questions.explain: Matrix addition is entry-by-entry: top-left 2+1=3, top-right 3+0=3, bottom-left 1+4=5, bottom-right -1+2=1, giving [[3,3],[5,1]].

questions.q: When computing the product AB, how is the entry in row i, column j of the result found?
options: By taking the dot product of row i of A with column j of B
By adding row i of A to column j of B
By multiplying every entry of A by every entry of B and summing all of them
By multiplying the entry in row i, column j of A by the entry in row i, column j of B
questions.explain: Matrix multiplication combines a row of the left matrix with a column of the right matrix via a dot product -- it is not an entry-by-entry operation.

questions.q: For A = [[2,3],[1,-1]] and B = [[1,0],[4,2]], the lesson computes AB = [[14,6],[-3,-2]] and BA = [[2,3],[10,10]]. What does this demonstrate?
options: Matrix multiplication is not commutative -- AB and BA can be different matrices
The lesson made an arithmetic error, since AB should always equal BA
A and B are not valid matrices because their product changes with order
questions.explain: AB = [[14,6],[-3,-2]] while BA = [[2,3],[10,10]] -- two different matrices from the same two inputs, concretely proving matrix multiplication is order-dependent.

questions.q: Why does the non-commutativity of matrix multiplication matter for quantum circuits specifically?
options: It doesn't matter for quantum circuits -- only for abstract math problems
Because each gate is a matrix, and applying gate A then gate B generally gives a different physical result than applying B then A, so circuit order is physically meaningful
Because non-commutative matrices cannot be applied to vectors at all
Because quantum computers cannot physically execute matrices in any particular order
questions.explain: Since gates are matrices and matrix multiplication isn't commutative, swapping the order of two gates in a circuit generally changes the final quantum state -- order is a real physical detail, not notation.

questions.q: Using M = [[2,1],[0,3]] and v = (4,5), what is Mv?
questions.explain: Row 1 dotted with v: (2)(4)+(1)(5)=13. Row 2 dotted with v: (0)(4)+(3)(5)=15. So Mv = (13, 15), matching the matrix-vector multiplication rule.
